data.title: The pagan faith of the Slavs and its evidence in archaeological finds
data.excerpt: The original religious ideas of the Slavs are reconstructed from sanctuaries and sacrificial sites, from idols and small cult figurines, from the burial rite and from magical symbols on pottery, tools, weapons and jewellery. This overview, taken from Zdeněk Váňa’s 1988 study, sorts that evidence into two layers of spiritual life - cult and magic.
data.metaTitle: The pagan faith of the Slavs in archaeological finds
data.metaDescription: Evidence for the original religion of the Slavs: sanctuaries, sacrificial sites, idols and cult figurines, the burial rite and magical symbols on pottery.

keyFacts.label: Subject
keyFacts.value: Archaeological evidence of cult and magic among the Slavs - sanctuaries, idols, talismans and symbols

timeline.title: Slavic culture takes shape
timeline.description: In the area north of the Carpathians, Slavic culture and the ethnic group are formed, together with the Indo-European legacy of the rite of cremating the dead.

timeline.title: The hoard from Martynovka
timeline.description: Sheet-metal figurines of bearded men are made - among the earliest evidence of small cult sculpture among the Slavs.

timeline.title: The peak of sanctuary building
timeline.description: Several attested cult buildings are erected - the temple on the Gross Raden hillfort, the sanctuaries at Stará Kouřim and at Pohansko near Břeclav, and the cult place at Mikulčice.

timeline.title: The transition to inhumation burial
timeline.description: In accordance with social differentiation, the graves tend to be richly furnished with jewellery, weapons and vessels - evidence of a more material conception of the afterlife.

timeline.title: The testimony of Ibn Fadlan
timeline.description: The Arab traveller describes the funeral of a Rus prince by cremation, which attests the connection of this rite with the idea of the higher value of posthumous existence.

timeline.title: The veneration of the Zbruch idol
timeline.description: On the Bogit hillfort the Zbruch idol was venerated, placed in a sacrificial site surrounded by a stone circle with eight sacrificial pits.

timeline.title: The two-headed idol from Fischerinsel
timeline.description: The find at a settlement near Neubrandenburg attests the cult of a twin deity among the Slavs.

timeline.title: Publication of the study
timeline.description: Zdeněk Váňa published the study “Archeologické doklady kultu a magie u Slovanů” in the journal Slovenská archeológia (XXXVI-2).

children.text: In recent years the original religious ideas of the Slavs have been becoming the focus of increased interest among archaeologists, historians, linguists and ethnographers. Archaeological excavation contributes to this, as do the discoveries of sanctuaries and sacrificial sites, finds of cult figures and objects, the evidence of the burial rite, of magical practices, of symbols and ideograms in the decoration of pottery, tools, weapons and jewellery. The interpretation of these material sources is often debatable, it is true, especially when it proceeds only from the things themselves and does not pay sufficient regard to the historical framework of the period and to ethnographic parallels. Archaeological excavation, however, has an indisputable priority in obtaining new facts, which fill the gaps in the written sources on which historical and linguistic study draws.

From a comparison of the individual kinds of sources we may also arrive at a relative distinction between two basic layers of spiritual life and the features that served its purposes: cult and magic. The boundary between the two is not, it is true, a very sharp one, and the two spheres often interpenetrate. Nevertheless, cult belongs essentially to the higher layer of religious ideas, bound up with reverence for natural or tribal deities, with sacrificial or possibly temple service, performed in the interest of the wider community by its leader - the prince or the priest as the representative of a social element that developed only among the Elbe and Baltic Slavs. Magical practices, by contrast, always relate rather to the undergrowth of every religious system; they invoke lower, elemental forces and beings, and are meant to protect against their unfavourable influences (apotropaic elements) or, conversely, to make use of them for the benefit of the individual, the family or the village, or with their help to harm others (in so-called black magic). This lower sphere of demonolatry was always the domain of sorcerers and their female counterparts (seeresses and diviners), who, unlike the cult element, survived even after the demise of paganism, often right up to the modern era, and therefore provide rich ethnographic material for comparison with archaeological finds.
Sanctuaries

The most striking evidence of cult are cult places and temples, relatively often mentioned in the written sources, especially in the area of the Elbe-Baltic and the Eastern Slavs. Archaeologically, however, it has been possible to identify these reports in only two cases: at Peryn in Russia and at Wolin on the Baltic. Peryn documents a typical Slavic open-air sacrificial site, with the cult of an idol of Perun surrounded by a circular symbolic ditch, whereas at Wolin it is a wooden, roofed building, a temple proper, of the kind attested both historically and archaeologically only in the area of the north-western Slavs.

The remaining discoveries are without exception historically anonymous. The feature on the Feldberg hillfort was evidently a temple: a simple rectangular building with a hint of an entrance space, separated from the hillfort by a symbolic ditch. The sanctuary that was discovered on the hillfort at Gross Raden in Mecklenburg, however, certainly was one, and it is readily reconstructable given the state of preservation of its remains. It was a building with an area of 7 × 11 m, with double walls and a walkway with a light balustrade, dated to the 9th century.

More numerous are the open cult places and sacrificial sites, which are, however, without exception historically anonymous. Their form is considerably varied; they are sacred spaces delimited by a ditch or by some other symbolic enclosure. From the territory of present-day Slovakia the sanctuary at Most pri Bratislave is known. From Bohemia there belong here, for example, Stará Kouřim with a cult place on the shore of the Libuše pool, of the 9th century, and Burgenland near Mšeno with a square sacrificial site delimited by a ditch and a post-built enclosure of the same period. The feature from Pohansko near Břeclav, consisting of eight globular pits grouped in a circle around a ninth in the middle and with traces of an enclosure, is also dated to the 9th century; it evidently represents the chief deity surrounded by secondary deities. This feature directly illustrates Ibn Fadlan’s report about the Rus traders on the Volga, who prayed to a large idol that stood in the middle of smaller ones set around it in a circle. At Mikulčice too, one of the main Great Moravian centres, a cult place was discovered with a rectangular ground plan of 11.3 × 24 m, delimited by a gully left by a palisade enclosure with a hint of an entrance on the south-eastern side. In the empty interior space only two hearths and a few shallow circular pits were found, evidently indicating the presence of sacred trees, such as were venerated, according to Helmold, in the vicinity of Wagrian Stargard, likewise inside a palisade enclosure. Circular sacrificial sites, delimited by a ditch, a palisade or stones, are known not only from the area of the Baltic Slavs, southern Poland or northern Russian Peryn, but also from further East Slavic sites, without exception of the 8th–10th centuries, from the land of the Smolensk Krivichi, in the Pskov region, in Bukovina, in the land of the Radimichi, or in the Pripyat Polesia. Here, however, they appear, especially in the earlier period (6th–9th centuries)
Idols

Of interest, too, is the discovery on the Bogit hillfort, near the find spot of the well-known Zbruch idol. In the western part of the hillfort, which as a whole served cult purposes, there stood a sacrificial site surrounded by a stone circle with eight sacrificial pits; a quadrangular pit in its centre, lined with stones, indicated the place where the Zbruch idol, venerated at this spot in the 10th–13th centuries, originally stood. The discovery brings to the fore the question of the interpretation of the Zbruch stele, which has been the subject of discussion for more than a century. The most probable reading, though not in all its details, appears to be the cosmogonic one, at least as regards the three bands on the stele as a symbol of three worlds: the sky as the world of the gods, the land - the world of people, and the underworld - the world of the beings who bear the land. This is an idea widespread since antiquity across the whole Eurasian continent; compare, for example, the gods and the giants in ancient Greece, with the world of people always in the middle. The interpretation of the four divine figures, however, remains problematic. It can in no way be Svantovit, whose cult was confined to the Slavic Baltic and could hardly have reached so far to the south; the symbol of the horn and the fourfold nature of the figures are not in themselves sufficient for this interpretation. Also doubtful is the identification of the idol with Rod, based on the Old Russian translation and commentaries of the homilies of St Gregory (Slovo sv. Grigorij Bogoslova) and on some further treatises of the 11th–12th centuries. Váňa states that Rod evidently belonged only to the local deities of a lower category and that there is not the slightest indication that he played such a general role as some scholars ascribe to him; in the Tale of Bygone Years, for example, he is not mentioned at all.

There is also the question of whether the figure with the ring is female (Lada?) - for it seems to have a moustache - and whether the warrior with the sabre can be connected with Perun: these attributes could have belonged to another local war deity as well. What is decisive is the fact that all four figures are joined by a single hat, which indicates a single deity in four hypostases: the economic one - with the horn as a symbol of fertility and abundance; the martial one - with the attributes of the sabre and the horse; the cosmic one - the ring as a symbol of the sky or the sun; the fourth figure, without attributes, could represent the deity’s own, purely spiritual form, standing behind the specifications mentioned, through which it manifests itself in its earthly sphere of action. It is noteworthy that the lower panel beneath it, where the others have giants, is empty. Such a combining of the functions of individual deities characterises the final phase in the development of Slavic religion and indicates a relatively late origin for the Zbruch stele, which the archaeological excavation has confirmed.

The other stone idols known to date come without exception from the East Slavic area, though their Slavic origin is not entirely assured. They include the numerous, more closely undatable “babas”, which could also have been left by the nomadic Turko-Tatar tribes, or by Baltic and Finnic tribes. In the contact zones, however, cult reached beyond ethnic and often also chronological boundaries, so that even pre-Slavic idols remained objects of reverence into the Early Middle Ages.

Of the large wooden idols, which are so far known only from the area of the north-western Slavs, mention must be made above all of the old find from Altfriesack, on account of its dating by radiocarbon test to the Early Slavic period. It bears witness to a relatively advanced level of religious ideas already in this early period and refutes the conception of some scholars of an original prototheism among the Slavs, whose polytheism with a specification of deities was supposed to have developed only in the 10th century. Although the idol cannot be identified with certainty with any of the gods described in the sources, the opening for a separately fitted phallus attests the specific function of a deity of fertility. In the Scandinavian area the counterpart is Freyr, whose statue in the temple at Uppsala was, according to Adam of Bremen, distinguished by a large phallus. The phallic cult is also attested by finds of phalluses themselves, for example at Łęczyca, Opole or Wolin.

A valuable archaeological contribution to the discussion of Slavic paganism is also the find of a two-headed idol at a settlement of the 11th–12th centuries on Fischerinsel near Neubrandenburg. It bears witness to the cult of a twin deity, which also played an important role in other Indo-European religious systems, for example among the Indians, the Iranians, the Hittites, the Greeks (Kastor and Polydeukes) and the Romans (Castor and Pollux). For the Slavs it is not attested in any of the older sources. We may therefore regard the existence of the Twins among the Slavs as demonstrated, but their name is uncertain. Nor do the other finds of wooden idols (Braak, Behren - Lubchin, Jankowo) permit identification with known deities.

children.text: Figurines

Very numerous are the small figurines of godlings, of metal, wood and antler. They appear already in find assemblages of the Early Slavic period in the form of sheet-metal figurines of bearded men in the hoard from Martynovka of the 7th century, or from the time of the Slavic expansion into the Aegean area in Thessaly. Later finds in the East Slavic area come from Novgorod, Old Ryazan and also from Old Russian pagan burial mounds. They appear occasionally in the territory of the southern Slavs too, for example at Garvăn-Dinogetia in Romania or at Preslav in Bulgaria, but they are more frequent in the milieu of the Elbe-Baltic and Polish Slavs, for example Schwedt, Weggun, Merseberg, Wolin, Wiálioa, Opole. They are sometimes identified with historically known deities: for example the Novgorod figurines, which have analogies in the Scandinavian milieu as well, with Perun; the wooden figurine of phallic shape with four faces from Wolin with Svantovit, and so on. The question, however, is whether deities that were the object of an organised public cult could also be depicted for the needs of private adoration in dwellings, with which the finds of small sculptures are undoubtedly connected. Ebbo’s account of the larger and smaller idols that Otto of Bamberg was preparing to burn at Wolin, which were, however, stolen and hidden, would suggest this. For the most part they were evidently statuettes of household godlings, whose existence is attested by the written sources and whose cult survived long, into later folk culture. The written reports of the veneration of idols in Cosmas, in the Opatovice Homiliary and so on probably concern them as well. In some areas these beings of a lower order too could acquire many-headed forms, which symbolically multiplied their power (Wolin, Wišlica, Preslav). Pendants, such as the one from Preslav, or the sheet-metal figurines serving as belt ornaments (Martynovka), performed rather an apotropaic function in the category of amulets.
Cult objects

Other objects and insignia also served the cult, of which both written testimonies and archaeological sources tell. The reports of western chroniclers speak of sacred weapons, equipment and banners deposited in temples as the attributes or insignia of the deity concerned. Their statements are illustrated by some archaeological discoveries as well, although not always expressly in cult contexts. This concerns, for example, the well-known engraving of a horseman with a spear and banners on a stone of the defensive wall at Libušín, which has an analogy on the defensive wall at Preslav in Bulgaria, likewise dated to the 10th century. In both cases the banners bear signs, and the drawings evidently served as an apotropaion protecting the strength and impregnability of the wall. The pole finial from a princely grave of the 9th century from Stará Kouřim likewise attests not only the carrying of tassels and field standards into battle, but is also a badge of the sacredness of the ruler’s power. The reports of sacred weapons deposited in a temple are probably attested by the finds of two spears and the remains of a wooden shield during the excavation of the temple at Gross Raden in Mecklenburg. Compare with this the statements about the sacred spear at Wolin, about Gerovit’s gilded shield at Wolgast, about Svantovit’s sword, bridle and saddle at Arkona. Reverence for sacred weapons was general among the Indo-Europeans - compare, for example, Thor’s hammer, Odin’s spear, Freyr’s sword among the Germanic peoples - and the Slavs were no exception in this respect.

blocks.alt: The pagan faith of the Slavs and its evidence in archaeological finds

children.text: From the milieu of both the Eastern and the Western Slavs, finds are reported of knives with a double volute in place of the handle, which were evidently used in killing sacrificial animals; they occur in Poland and in Slovakia as well. Wooden staves and clubs with carved heads in the form of human or animal heads, known for example from Novgorod, probably served for ritual dances and ceremonies, for instance at the rusalii. A scene of adoration is depicted on a sherd of an Early Slavic vessel found at Schulzendorf in the area of the Elbe Slavs: in a stabbed technique it shows schematically a human figure standing in a gesture of adoration before something that might be interpreted as a cauldron on a wagon, a boat, or an altar with an idol. The vessel undoubtedly served cult purposes. The gesture of prayer, of which we have only indirect hints, is relatively well attested archaeologically. It is the stance of the Orans, known already from pagan antiquity. It is borne, for example, by the relief figure on a sheet-metal mount from Pskov, by Gerovit’s stone from Wolgast and by the orantes from Mikulčice engraved on belt mounts: one of them represents, it is true, a Christian saint-priest in vestments, but the second is unquestionably pagan in character and does not depict a prince with insignia, as is sometimes supposed, but a sorcerer in a cult gesture with a horn of plenty and a shamanic mirror; the third Orans symbolises prayer alone, whether pagan or Christian. For the interpretation of these engravings it is above all their placing on the reverse of the mount that is decisive, indicating that the purpose was in all cases apotropaic and therefore belongs to the sphere of magic. The same may be said of the figure with raised arms depicted in stabbed dots on the sheath of a knife of bronze sheet from the Late Slavic cemetery at Schirmenitz. In this case too the gesture represents a plea for the protection of the knife’s owner. The properties of the cult also included leather or wooden masks, found for example in Novgorod and in Silesia. They were used in masquerade processions and games, especially within the festivities of the winter solstice, but besides that on other occasions as well, for instance weddings, funerals and the rusalii feasts. The original meaning of the mask was apotropaic: to frighten off demons, at the winter solstice to banish the spirits of darkness, and in the other cases to drive away the evil powers threatening the wedding guests or the souls of the dead.
The burial rite

A specifically archaeological contribution to the understanding of religious ideas is the evidence of the burial rite and of the cult of the dead. The rite of cremating the dead is an original Indo-European legacy, attested already in the ancient cultures in the area north of the Carpathians, out of which Slavic culture, and with it the ethnic group, was formed in the 5th–6th centuries. Together with the Slavic expansion, cremation then spread within the Early Slavic culture of the Prague, Korchak and related types to the Balkans and into central and Eastern Europe as one of its characteristic features. According to indirect analogies from other Indo-European cultures, and in part also according to the testimony of Ibn Fadlan, who witnessed the funeral of a Rus prince in the 10th century, the cremation of the dead was bound up with the view that posthumous existence was of higher value, for which the dead physical body was an obstacle tying one to the earth and which therefore had to be destroyed by fire. This view need not necessarily be connected with belief in a supreme deity in the sense of monotheism, as some authors judge, because it accompanies polytheistic systems as well; among the Slavs, according to the testimony of Procopius of the 6th century, one may rather infer henotheism, with the rule of a supreme god over the others. The burial rite expresses only ideas about the afterlife and nothing more, so that the transition to the burial of unburnt bodies may be understood as an expression of a relatively greater attachment to the values of earthly life. Among the Slavs it occurs first under the influence of a more intensive symbiosis with nomadic tribes, as is attested also by the vampiric notion of the “living corpse” taken over from there, likewise abundantly attested archaeologically.

children.text: The relationship to the deceased and to his posthumous existence is also manifested in the grave goods placed in the grave. Whereas with the cremation rite these were mostly small objects from the personal property of the dead person (brooches, buckles, small knives, fire-steels and the like), with so-called inhumation burial in the 8th–10th centuries the graves were, in accordance with social differentiation, often richly furnished with jewellery, weapons, tools and vessels with food and drink. This fact too bears witness to a more material conception of the afterlife and its physical needs, together with the fundamental change of rite. Ethnographic sources, after all, speak of this as well: according to them the dead person, appearing as a shadowy figure, can speak, move, leave behind the traces of hands and feet, eat, drink and even have sexual intercourse.
Talismans

Relatively numerous are the finds of small objects which by their shape or decoration go beyond purely practical purposes and belong to the sphere of magic and its practices. Already in the Early Slavic culture there appear clay objects of disc-like or loaf-like shape, which undoubtedly played a certain role in magic of the creative type, in which the depiction of an object, in this case evidently bread, was to ensure its abundance. Two fragments from Libušín in Bohemia bear on both sides a stabbed motif of a cross in a circle, one of the series of symbols of the sun as an indicator of space and a measure of time (the four cardinal points and the four seasons); the smaller one has a hint of a double cross, the so-called “black cross”, which performed an apotropaic function in later folk culture as well. The creative practices of folk magic are also graphically illustrated by the inexpertly formed figurines of animals, people and saddles from the earlier phase of the Great Moravian centre at Mikulčice, usually interpreted as votive offerings (for which, however, the corresponding sacrificial site is lacking). The majority of the finds of animal figurines evidently fall into the same category, if some of them did not serve as children’s toys. The horse was a sacred animal consecrated to the gods, for example to Svantovit, Svarožič and Triglav, and therefore undoubtedly performed a magical, apotropaic function, both in plastic and in drawn renderings on various objects: jewellery, combs, fire-steels, vessels, pendants, amulets and the like.

blocks.alt: The pagan faith of the Slavs and its evidence in archaeological finds

children.text: It must be stressed that early medieval art and craft, which preserved the old pagan symbolism even after the acceptance of Christianity, often right into late folk culture, performed not only a decorative but also a magical function, with a certain inner meaning for the person who used these things, whether in an apotropaic sense, for protection against the unfavourable forces of nature and of fate, or to ensure success in productive activity, in trade, in battle and in personal matters. For this reason we regard in the same way, besides the horse as an independent figure or on various objects, other animal motifs as well: fish, birds, lambs, goats, snakes, deer, dragons, griffins, and possibly also mythical beings such as rusalki and sirens, or the motifs of the tree of life, the horn of plenty, sun ideograms and the like. We encounter them particularly often on Russian bracelets and pendants, which also had the apotropaic function of talismans. Around the neck hung spoons as a symbol of satiety and prosperity, keys as a symbol of safety and wealth, axes as an attribute of Perun, combs ensuring protection against disease, lunulae connected with the cult of the moon, animal teeth, claws and jaws, rattles and cowrie shells, without exception as protection against harmful forces. Many of these motifs can be seen on jewellery and ornaments in the most varied renderings from other Slavic cultural areas as well: Slavic-Avar, Bijelo Brdo, Carantanian, Bulgarian, Great Moravian, Bohemian, Polish and Elbe-Baltic.

Clay eggs with a coloured glaze also served magical purposes; they were made already in the 10th century chiefly in Kievan Rus, but were widespread in other places as well, for example at Opole in Silesia, at Wolin in Pomerania, at Gdańsk and elsewhere. They symbolised the power of fertility and it may be assumed that they were used above all in wedding ceremonies.
Symbols

A separate group of magical motifs is formed by ideograms, graphic symbols: the circle, the cross, the swastika, the svarga, the triquetra, the bicycle, the rosette, lunulae, the pentagram, the hexagram, the hand and their variants. They appear on vessels, jewellery, weapons, tools, stones and other objects with a quite obvious magical function, protective and creative. They are widespread across all continents, in some cases as early as the Palaeolithic, without cultural, ethnic or chronological boundaries, as a kind of ancient world script which, in its multiplicity of meanings, was understood without words. They expressed the experience of the forces of nature and at the same time the idea that these forces act through their symbol as well, which was their concentration: an ideogram placed on the base of a vessel protected the food and multiplied it; on a sword or an axe it gave the warrior greater strength; on spindle whorls, a firm thread; on pendants, finger rings or a bracelet it protected the owner against evil forces, and so on.

That is also why these ideograms survived in Christian culture too, which often gave them merely a different meaning, as in the case of the cross, and we encounter them in folk culture as well, often right up to the present day: on folk costumes, embroidery, painted Easter eggs, jewellery, furniture, chests, lamps, sledges, wagons, beams, and the windows and doors of dwellings, in potters’ and masons’ marks and the like.

The article was taken over, with only minimal editing, from Zdeněk Váňa’s study Archeologické doklady kultu a magie u Slovanů (Archaeological evidence of cult and magic among the Slavs; Slovenská archeológia XXXVI-2, 1988).
